finding: Strong math solvers are poor scaffolders. Solving skill and tutoring skill trade off.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct scores about 0.88-0.91 on problem solving but only 0.06 win rate on scaffolding generation. The scaffolding reward model (ModernBERT-based) reaches 0.84 accuracy at ranking expert over novice teacher replies.
limits: High-school math only. Dialogs up to 10 turns. Judge is a learned reward model, not learning outcomes.
agent_relevance: A strong model is not automatically a good scaffold giver. A scaffold role must be built and checked on its own, not assumed from solve accuracy.

finding: General LLM-as-judge and general reward models barely detect good pedagogy. Only a model fine-tuned on pedagogical preference data does.
numbers: LLM-as-judge accuracy below 0.7 on expert-vs-novice pairs. RewardBench reward models only slightly above chance. Fine-tuned on MathDial plus MRBench pairs: 0.84. Synthetic GSM8K-inpainted pairs gave 0.60.
limits: Preference data is mostly model generations; few human-teacher responses.
agent_relevance: If our agent needs a judge of 'is this hint a scaffold or a leak', use a task-specific checker, not a general judge (fits G5).

finding: Telling the model to scaffold (pedagogical instruction following) helps GPT-4o but not most other models. Tutoring gets harder in longer dialogs.
numbers: GPT-4o gained significantly on the hard split with pedagogical instructions. SocraticLM, LearnLM and Llama models stayed flat or dropped. Only LearnLM kept stable results across differing student states.
limits: Per-model deltas not quoted; read from text of section 6.1.
agent_relevance: A scaffold prompt works only on models that follow it. Test instruction following before relying on a prompt-level scaffold.

source: Liu et al. (2025) GuideEval, Discerning Minds or Generic Tutors
finding: LLMs do not adapt scaffolding to learner state. They fail when the learner is confused or wrong and needs redirection.
numbers: Education model SocraticLM: perception-of-error score 0.1411 and orchestration-reconfigure 0.0712, versus roughly 0.4-0.78 for general models. Some general models affirm correct reasoning at 0.9+ but flag erroneous reasoning at under 0.5 (row labels in the extracted table may be shifted; the SocraticLM row is explicit).
limits: Benchmark built from real dialogues. LLM judge agrees with human labels 89.0-97.0% of the time across 7 criteria.
agent_relevance: Model is good at affirming and weak at noticing a wrong learner step. For our agent, a code check must flag the failing step (G2), not the model.

source: Liu et al. (2025) GuideEval, Discerning Minds or Generic Tutors
finding: Teaching a small model the scaffolding behaviour helps, and process-level supervision helps most.
numbers: Qwen3-8B base vs rule prompt, SFT, KTO, DPO, SFT with CoT distillation: CoT-distilled SFT gave the strongest gains in most cases. Plain SFT hurt instructional strategy. KTO gave little contrast. DPO helped state recognition.
limits: Exact figures only in a chart (not extractable). Fine-tuning is outside our no-training constraint.
agent_relevance: What the learner state is matters more than the final utterance. Log state, not just output.

source: Wei et al. (2026) UCO, adaptive teaching with RL
finding: A reward for staying inside the learner's zone of proximal development (ZPD) improves a 7B tutor. The ZPD is estimated from entropy of the student's answer states.
numbers: BigMath: UCO 7B solve rate 30.2%, answer leak 12.9%, pedagogy reward model 4.6/4.5. Strongest teaching baseline Qwen2.5-7B-RL leaks 27.5% (14.6 points worse). GPT-4o: 33.1% solve, 35.2% leak. DeepSeek-V3: 39.3% solve, 46.6% leak.
limits: Simulated students, math only, RL training.
agent_relevance: Direct operational definition of ZPD: pick the hint level one step below what the learner can already do.

source: Wei et al. (2026) UCO, adaptive teaching with RL
finding: Ablation: removing the ZPD scaffold reward hurts most. Larger general models leak more answers.
numbers: Without scaffold reward on BigMath: solve 23.5% (-6.7), leak 20.2% (+7.3), pedagogy 2.2/2.3. Without progress reward: solve 28.6%, leak 15.6%, pedagogy 4.1/3.9. On MathTutorBench removing scaffold reward cost -3.4 (expertise), -9.0 (student understanding), -10.6 (pedagogy). Qwen2.5 7B to 72B: solve 11.3 to 38.7%, leak 29.3 to 61.0%.
limits: Single paper, author-built metrics; v4 revised 2026.
agent_relevance: Bigger helper means more telling. If a stronger model provides hints in our loop, cap how much it may reveal.

finding: Stepwise hints from a helper model lift small reasoning models. This is a direct software form of scaffolding.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B on NuminaMath 46.67% to 78.67% with LLM hints (+32.00); AIME-2024 13.79% to 41.38%. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B AIME-2024 20.69% to 68.97% (+48.28) with LLM hints; with a fine-tuned 7B hinter 34.48%.
limits: LLM hints were built from the ground-truth full solution (GPT-5.2, human checked), so this is an oracle upper bound. AIME-2024 has 29 problems and AIME-2025 has 15, so one problem is 3-7 points.
agent_relevance: Shows the ceiling of external scaffolding: gains are huge when the hint giver knows the answer. Our agent has no oracle, so expect much less.

finding: A fine-tuned small hinter that cannot solve the problem still helps. Untrained hinters hurt in places. Gains do not always hold.
numbers: SLM hints: MATH-500 R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 64.86% to 85.14% (beat LLM hints 82.43%). Untrained (NFT) hints often hurt: Qwen2.5-Math-7B MATH-500 75.68% to 54.05%, NuminaMath 46.67% to 36.00%. AIME-2025 unchanged for several models (13.33% to 13.33%).
limits: Small N; AIME-2025 is noise. Hint quality, not hint presence, drives the effect.
agent_relevance: Bad scaffolds are worse than none. A hint step needs a quality gate.

finding: Stepwise hinting beats self-consistency on cost and, on hard items, on accuracy.
numbers: R1-Distill-Qwen-7B: MATH-500 no-hint 64.86%, HintMR 82.43%, SC (K=8) 70.27%; AIME-2024 20.69%, 68.97%, 20.69%. Tokens: SC 7350 vs HintMR 1180 on MATH-500; time 689s vs 165s.
limits: HintMR row uses a hinter trained with oracle-derived hints.
agent_relevance: Structured guidance can replace brute-force sampling, consistent with G4 (samples are not independent).

source: Kim et al. (2025) SMART, Guiding Reasoning in SLMs with LLM Assistance
finding: Calling the helper only at low-confidence steps keeps most of the benefit. This is fading scaffolding: help only where the learner is stuck.
numbers: Small model plus selective LLM step replacement reaches up to 98.9% of LLM accuracy with up to 90.0% fewer LLM tokens (MATH500). Best-of-N, Qwen: level 5 problems 99.12% of LLM accuracy (+73.20% over the small model); level 1 +5.20%.
limits: Needs a step scorer (token confidence or process reward model). Math only.
agent_relevance: Matches the Vygotsky idea of help only where needed. An impasse signal decides when to call the helper (fits G1).

source: Kim et al. (2025) SMART, Guiding Reasoning in SLMs with LLM Assistance
finding: Gain from help rises with problem difficulty.
numbers: Llama 1B-8B beam search level 5: 114.57% of LLM accuracy (+39.23%); Best-of-N level 5 94.94% (+141.55%). Levels 1-2 gains small (+2.5 to +15%).
limits: Relative-to-LLM numbers can exceed 100% because they are ratios.
agent_relevance: Scaffold only the hard items; easy items need no extra steps.

finding: LLMs cannot judge what is within a child's reach. Zero-shot, some models fall below chance when grading reading difficulty by school stage.
numbers: 60 Special-Grade teachers annotated a 3-way label (elementary, middle, high). Zero-shot: GLM and Qwen-max under 33% accuracy (chance 33%); Qwen32B 63.14%. Elementary accuracy for Qwen-max 9.83%, GLM 7.71%. GLM put 88.03% of texts in middle school.
limits: Chinese reading, 10 models. Direction bias: Qwen-Plus and GPT-4o WDBI above 0.4 (overestimate difficulty, underestimate students).
agent_relevance: The model does not know where the learner's level is. Our agent must estimate level from observed attempts, not from the model's belief.

finding: Two in-context examples fix much of the gap.
numbers: Qwen-max accuracy 30.61% to 62.96%; GLM 26.59% to 68.78%; DeepSeek-V3 F1 83.52%, accuracy 0.8313. Absolute average bias (WDBI) down 14% (to 0.2317). Three models that over-estimated got worse.
limits: Fix is partial; bias direction can flip.
agent_relevance: Few-shot calibration is cheap but must be tested for the bias direction per model.

source: Figueiredo (2025) Fuzzy logic prompting for adaptive tasks
finding: A prompt with ZPD-style boundary and fuzzy support-level rules improves scaffolding quality and adaptivity over flat and few-shot prompts, in simulation.
numbers: Rubric scores (LLM graders, synthetic K-12 learner profiles): scaffolding vs flat d=0.41, vs few-shot d=0.45 (p<.001); adaptivity d=0.41 and 0.46 (p<.001); grade match not significant (p=0.485, d=0.22-0.24).
limits: Simulated learners, LLM graders, no human learners. Moderate effects only.
agent_relevance: A prompt-only scaffold gives moderate but real gains in adaptivity. It needs an external grader, which is weak (G5).

source: Cohn et al. (2026) Theory of Adaptive Scaffolding, Inquizzitor
finding: A theory-grounded assessment agent was faithful to ZPD-style feedback most of the time in real classroom data, but weak at goal setting.
numbers: ZPD faithfulness (first column group, my reading of the table) 79.83% (FA2), 78.22% (FA3), 88.57% (FA4); unfaithful 20.17%, 21.78%, 11.43%. Agent gave in to off-task trickery in 4-5% of utterances; changed scores in under 1% of cases. Mean reading level FKGL 6.6.
limits: Middle-school Earth science, no randomized trial, LLM judges plus human checks.
agent_relevance: Even a well-prompted scaffolder drifts under pressure from the learner; keep scoring decisions in code.

finding: Randomized trial: LLM-supplied expert-style hints to human tutors raised student mastery, mostly for weaker tutors. A scaffold for the scaffolder.
numbers: 700+ tutors, 1,000+ students. Exit-ticket pass 62% to 66% (+4 points, p<.01). Lower-rated tutors: 56% to 65% (+9). Less experienced tutors 61% to 68% (+7). On-treated estimate +14 points. Cost about $20 per tutor per year. 350,000+ messages: more probing questions, less generic praise.
limits: Math tutoring, one platform. Effects shrink as tutor skill rises.
agent_relevance: Gain is largest where base skill is lowest. A scaffold helps a weak agent more than a strong one.

source: Bastani et al. (2025) Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning
finding: Unrestricted GPT-4 raised practice scores but lowered later exam scores. A guarded tutor (solution plus common mistakes in the prompt, told not to give answers) removed the harm but added no learning.
numbers: About 1,000 Turkish high-school students, four 90-minute sessions. Practice: GPT Tutor +127%, GPT Base +48%. Unassisted exam: GPT Base -17% vs control; GPT Tutor about equal to control.
quote: Students attempt to use GPT-4 as a 'crutch'.
limits: Working-paper text read; PNAS 2025 version (vol 122, e2422633122) gives the same 48% and 127% in its abstract. One country, one subject.
agent_relevance: Help that does the work removes the learning. In an agent, a scaffold that supplies answers will not store a lesson; the lesson must come from the attempt.

source: Scarlatos et al. (2025) Training LLM-based tutors to improve student learning outcomes
finding: Training the tutor on a simulated student's next-answer correctness (plus a pedagogy rubric) beats prompting on predicted student success.
numbers: MathDial test: DPO-trained 8B tutor improves predicted student correctness by 33% over the next best method, GPT-4o, and matches GPT-4o on the pedagogy rubric. Student-correctness predictor AUC 0.76.
limits: Outcome is a simulated student, not real learners. Withholding the answer is a rubric item.
agent_relevance: Learner-outcome reward (not text quality) is the right target for a scaffold.

finding: Decomposing a task into easier sub-questions solved in order, each reusing earlier answers, is a prompt-level scaffold. It turns failure into near-perfect scores on length generalization.
numbers: SCAN length split, code-davinci-002: standard 16.7%, chain-of-thought 16.2%, least-to-most 99.7%; text-davinci-002 76.0% vs CoT 0.0%. GSM8K overall: 60.97% to 62.39%; for problems needing 5+ steps 39.07% to 45.23%.
limits: Gain depends on a good decomposition prompt; GSM8K failures were mostly solvable with manual decomposition. SCAN is synthetic.
agent_relevance: Worth-taking operator: ask for sub-steps in order and feed each answer forward.

finding: An automatic curriculum (next task just beyond current skills) plus a skill library of past solved tasks drives an LLM agent far beyond baselines.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 iterations, 3.3x baselines; wooden tool 15.3x, stone 8.5x, iron 6.4x faster; only agent reaching diamond. Random curriculum cuts discovered items by 93%; without the skill library progress plateaus.
limits: Minecraft; GPT-4 needed (GPT-3.5 much worse).
agent_relevance: Closest working machine form of ZPD plus stored scaffolds: pick the next problem just past ability and retrieve earlier solved skills.

finding: Stored lessons (distilled insights) and retrieved past trajectories help in different tasks and together beat either alone.
numbers: Insights-only vs retrieve-only success: HotpotQA 36% vs 31%, ALFWorld 50% vs 55%, WebShop 37% vs 38%. ALFWorld with Reflexion rounds: retrieve-only 40.3% to 54.4% by round 3; ExpeL+Reflexion 54.5% to 60.4%. Transfer HotpotQA insights to FEVER: ReAct 58, ExpeL transfer 65 (63 without task demos).
limits: Table cell labels in the extracted text are partly ambiguous; the figures given are the ones clearly labeled.
agent_relevance: Lessons as reusable scaffolds do transfer across tasks (memory design note).

finding: Verbal self-reflection stored in memory works as self-scaffolding on later tries.
numbers: Absolute gains of 22% on AlfWorld in 12 learning steps, 20% on HotpotQA, 11% on HumanEval; HumanEval pass@1 91% vs 80% for GPT-4. Self-reflection gave an 8% absolute boost over episodic memory alone.
limits: Needs a reliable external signal; weak when feedback is unreliable (false-positive test rate matters).
agent_relevance: Revise only from real output (G2). Reflection text is a scaffold for the next attempt.

source: Acquaye et al. (2026) Take Out Your Calculators, LLM student simulations
finding: LLMs play weaker students better if they are themselves weaker. Role-play at set skill levels predicts item difficulty far better than asking directly.
numbers: Role-play plus item response theory: correlation up to 0.75, 0.76, 0.82 (grades 4, 8, 12). Direct text-based difficulty prediction is weak (about 0.36 at grade 4, 0.30 at grade 12, -0.04 at grade 8). Gemma models r about 0.66-0.70; Llama-3-8b about 0.42-0.44.
limits: NAEP math multiple choice only.
agent_relevance: Strong models cannot reliably be set to act weak. Our agent should not simulate a lower-level self by prompt alone.

finding: Assistant-tuned LLMs give overly advanced answers when asked to play weaker students. A knowledge-graph prototype of the student plus beam-search refinement fixes much of it.
numbers: Authors report about 100% improvement in simulation accuracy and realism over prompt baselines; behavior prediction accuracy reaches 0.94 at 40 past records.
limits: Datasets of 15 and 100 simulated students; improvement figure as stated in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Learner model needs record-based state, not a persona prompt (G4).

source: Wood, Bruner & Ross (1976) The role of tutoring in problem solving
finding: Founding scaffolding study: adults helped 3-5 year olds build a pyramid and showed six tutor functions (recruit, reduce degrees of freedom, keep direction, mark critical features, control frustration, demonstrate).
numbers: Not opened this session; details from background knowledge, no figures quoted.
limits: Not read; do not cite numbers from this line.
agent_relevance: Source for the six tutor operators that the LLM scaffolding papers above measure.
